planting.note: Plant corms 2 inches deep in fall in sandy, sharply drained coastal soil in full sun; this low winter-growing species from Cape sand dunes and flats needs a strictly dry summer rest.

directions: Plant corms about 2 inches deep in fall in sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun, siting them where winter rains can reach them but summer irrigation cannot. This diminutive coastal species rarely exceeds a few inches in height, yet its blue-to-violet flowers are disproportionately large for the plant, each lower tepal marked with a bold white patch bordered in deeper violet. Flowering runs from late winter into early spring, after which the foliage dies back and the corms must be kept bone dry through the hot months to avoid rot. Its small scale makes it best suited to raised sand beds, troughs, or pots grown alongside other dwarf Cape bulbs.

planting.note: Plant corms 2 inches deep in fall in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this rare Western Cape species is now known from only a small area around Hopefield and should be sourced from cultivated, not wild-collected, stock.

directions: Plant corms shallowly in fall in lean, sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun, allowing the hairy, lance-shaped leaves to grow through the cool, wet Cape winter. Large, cheerful yellow flowers with a dark purplish-brown central blotch open in late winter into early spring on a plant that rarely tops a few inches, giving an outsized floral display relative to its diminutive stature. Once flowering finishes the plant needs a completely dry summer dormancy, so it is best grown in a container that can be kept under cover once the leaves yellow. Because wild populations are now confined to a very small area near Hopefield, gardeners should grow only nursery-propagated corms and treat this as a conservation-minded collector's plant rather than a mass bedding subject.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in deep sandy soil in full sun; this Western Cape species grows in coastal and inland dunes and needs a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in deep, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, replicating the coastal and inland dune habitats where this species naturally grows in the Western Cape. Sweetly to spicily scented, dark blue-to-mauve flowers open in late winter and early spring, each lower tepal marked with a creamy-white patch outlined by a more intense violet band, making it one of the more richly colored and fragrant of the smaller babianas. Like its relatives, it needs a bone-dry summer rest once the linear leaves die back, so container culture or a raised, unirrigated bed works best outside its native winter-rainfall climate. Its fragrance and compact size make it a good companion for other dwarf Cape corms in a bulb frame or trough.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck near soil level in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; unlike most garden nerines this wide-ranging interior species is summer-growing and winter-dormant, matching the summer-rainfall climate of the Free State, Northern Cape, Namibia, and Botswana.

directions: Plant the large, deep-seated bulbs with their necks near soil level in spring, in well-drained sandy to loamy soil in full sun. Unlike the more familiar autumn-flowering Cape nerines, this wide-ranging interior species follows the opposite, summer-rainfall growing cycle of its native Free State, Northern Cape, Namibia, and Botswana range, sending up broad, strap-shaped leaves and short-lived umbels of white to pale pink flowers with a faint pinkish-brown midrib during the warmer months. Because it is adapted to cold, dry winters rather than mild wet ones, it should be kept nearly dry once dormant and protected from hard freezes where grown outside its native range. Its large, spherical flower heads and tolerance of a more continental climate make it a useful nerine for gardeners whose conditions don't suit the winter-growing Cape species.

planting.note: Plant bulbs shallowly after last frost in gritty, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this high-elevation Drakensberg species prefers cooler summer conditions than lowland pineapple lilies.

directions: Plant bulbs shallowly after the soil has warmed in spring, in gritty but moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, watering regularly through summer since this species grows naturally on wet rock faces and grassy basalt slopes at high elevation in the Drakensberg. It forms a tiny rosette of only three or four prostrate leaves, their undersides tinged maroon, from which a very short spike of dull dark red to purple flowers with contrasting purple stamens emerges in midsummer. Its high-elevation origin makes it more tolerant of cool nights and summer moisture than most other pineapple lilies, but it still needs sharp drainage and a drier winter rest. Given its tiny stature, it is best grown in a trough, alpine pan, or the front of a rock garden where it won't be overshadowed by larger neighbors.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle, blooming in late winter to spring before going summer dormant.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, letting the wiry stems grow through the cool Cape winter. Known locally as bloukalossie ('blue stocking'), this species sends up long, slender wands topped with star-shaped flowers in shades of blue, mauve, or violet-purple, making an excellent, long-lasting cut flower. Like other winter-growing corn lilies, it goes fully dormant once summer heat arrives and should be kept dry until autumn rains, or watering, resume. Its taller, more willowy habit than many ixia hybrids suits informal drifts among other Cape bulbs rather than tight, formal plantings.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; a grassland and open-woodland species from South Africa's winter-rainfall regions.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them to allow slender stalks to lean gracefully without support. Clusters of three to five bright, apricot-orange, star-shaped flowers, each with a dark purple central eye, open atop wiry stems in spring, giving a warmer color than the blue and pink tones common in many other corn lilies. The plant is drought-tolerant once established and, like other South African corn lilies, requires a dry summer dormancy to persist from year to year. Its bright orange color and compact habit make it a good accent among cooler-toned ixia and sparaxis plantings.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in loamy, sandy, or gravelly soil in full sun; corms are renewed annually and resprout with autumn and winter rains.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in loam, sand, or ironstone-gravel soil in full sun, mimicking the free-draining substrates this species favors in the wild. Tall, branching stems carry cream, yellow, and soft orange star-shaped flowers in late winter into early autumn depending on locality, with the whole plant dying back to a renewed corm once flowering finishes. Because the corms are essentially replaced each year rather than persisting indefinitely, gardeners in marginal climates can treat it much like a true annual bulb, lifting and storing corms over the dry or cold season. Its taller, airier flower spikes work well toward the back of a Cape bulb border or in a cutting garden.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

common_name: Red Bugle Lily (Van der Spuy's Watsonia)

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; one of the largest watsonias, so allow ample room for its tall sword-shaped foliage and flower spikes.

directions: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving this Northern and Western Cape native plenty of room since its glossy, sword-shaped leaves and flower spikes can reach 6 feet or more, among the largest in the genus. Vivid orange-red, funnel-shaped flowers open in succession up the tall spikes, a display so gladiolus-like that the close family relationship between the two genera is immediately obvious. Like other Cape watsonias, it grows through the cooler, wetter months and rests through the hottest part of summer, so established plantings should not be watered heavily once foliage begins to decline. Its imposing size makes it a dramatic accent at the back of a mixed bulb border rather than a plant for small spaces.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in spring in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; unlike most watsonias this Western Cape fynbos species is summer-growing and often flowers most heavily after fire.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in spring in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun, since this species grows on dry mountain slopes among rock outcrops rather than in rich garden loam. Solitary, unbranched spikes bear numerous large, scarlet-to-orange trumpet flowers in mid-to-late summer, appearing like beacons scattered through the surrounding fynbos, often flowering most profusely in the seasons following a wildfire. Its stiff, sword-shaped leaves have distinctly thickened margins that help it withstand the exposed, wind-scoured sites it favors in habitat. Because it is adapted to a summer-growing, rocky-slope lifestyle rather than a rich, moist border, it performs best with sharp drainage and minimal supplemental water once established.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in heavier, clay-loam soil that is seasonally wet in winter but dry in summer, in full sun; found naturally on waterlogged clay flats near Caledon in the southwestern Cape.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in heavier clay-loam soil in full sun, since this species naturally grows on clay flats and slopes near Caledon that are seasonally waterlogged in winter, unlike the sandy soils preferred by many other Cape corms. Radially symmetrical flowers in buff to yellow tones, often flushed mauve on the reverse, open on short stems from late winter into early spring. Because it tolerates more moisture-retentive soil during its growing season than most sparaxis, it can be a useful choice for a heavier garden bed where drainage is imperfect, provided the site still dries out completely in summer. Give it full sun and a summer rest to keep the corms healthy from year to year.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in dry, stony clay soil in full sun; native to the Northwest Cape and Roggeveld, an area with a shorter, more arid winter growing season than the wetter southwestern Cape.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in dry, stony, clay-based soil in full sun, reflecting the harsher, more arid Roggeveld and Northwest Cape habitat this species comes from compared to wetter southwestern Cape sparaxis. The short-tubed, bilaterally symmetrical flowers are noted for a sweet fragrance reminiscent of freesias, a trait shared by few other harlequin flowers, and appear from midwinter into early autumn depending on rainfall timing. Because it comes from a drier winter-rainfall region, it needs even less summer and winter moisture than most cultivated sparaxis and resents heavy or waterlogged soils. Its fragrance makes it worth growing near a path or seating area where the scent can be appreciated at close range.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in clay-rich Renosterveld-type soil in full sun to very light shade; a Red-Listed Western Cape endemic that has lost most of its habitat to agriculture, so source only nursery-propagated stock.

directions: Plant corms in fall in clay-rich soil in full sun to very light shade, replicating the Renosterveld habitat of this rare Western Cape endemic, which blooms best on recently disturbed or cleared ground. Sweetly scented, flared trumpet flowers in pale yellow to cream, marked with dull purple on the reverse and a touch of orange at the base of the lower tepals, open unusually early for a freesia, from midwinter into late summer in its native winter-rainfall range. Most of its natural habitat has been lost to agricultural conversion, so cultivated stock helps take pressure off wild populations while preserving the species in gardens. Grow it as you would other winter-growing Cape freesias, keeping it dry through its summer dormancy.
sources: SANBI Red List of South African Plants

planting.note: Plant corms in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; naturally grows wedged into cliff-face crevices in the Drakensberg, so excellent drainage is essential.

directions: Plant corms in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade after the last frost, mimicking the sheer Drakensberg cliff faces where this species naturally roots into crevices and ledges. Its common name, suicide lily, commemorates the risks early plant collectors took to reach it on dangerous rock faces rather than any trait of the plant itself. Short, arching spikes carry up to seven bright red, roughly two-inch flowers in succession through the warmer months, and the plant tolerates regular water while actively growing before going dormant and dry in late summer. It is more cold-tolerant than many tender South African gladiolus species and does well in a rock garden, raised bed, or trough where excess winter wet can be kept away from the corms.
